title: Rama's one wish
hook: Rama's father appears, and Rama spends his one wish on forgiveness

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fire. Sita called on Agni, the witness of every vow, and Agni gave her back. Today, Rama's one wish, and the flight home.

Before they leave Lanka, someone comes that Rama never expected to see again. His father. King Dasharatha, who died of grief after sending his son into exile, appears in the sky in a shining chariot. He holds Rama close for a long time, embraces Lakshmana too, and speaks kindly to Sita. And Rama, with his father in front of him at last, asks for one thing. Not for himself.

Long ago, in his grief, Dasharatha disowned Kaikeyi, who had demanded Rama's exile, and her son Bharata with her. Now Rama asks: take those words back. Be gracious to Kaikeyi and to Bharata. Dasharatha agrees. Think about who Rama is asking for. Kaikeyi's demand cost him fourteen years in the forest, and it broke his father's heart. Rama could ask for anything. He asks for her forgiveness. Hindus call Rama maryada purushottam, the ideal man, the one who lives dharma, right living, all the way through. And old Hindu lists of dharma's marks include kshama, forgiveness, right beside truth and self-control. Here it is in a single wish. Then Indra offers a gift, and again Rama asks for others: bring back the monkeys and bears who died for me, so they can see their families again. Indra grants it, and the fallen rise, whole. Now it's time to go. Rama promised Bharata he'd be back the day the fourteen years ended, and there's no time to walk. So Vibhishana brings out the Pushpaka, the flying chariot that once belonged to Kubera, god of wealth, until Ravana took it. It rises, huge and golden, and Rama points out the places below to Sita: there's where Ravana fell; there's the bridge, still crossing the sea. In many families, Diwali is the season of visits and sweets, and of calling the relative you've drifted from. Rama shows why that call is dharma, not just manners.
screen: `FORGIVE KAIKEYI AND BHARATA.` · `KSHAMA: A MARK OF DHARMA.` · `BRING BACK THE FALLEN.` · `THE PUSHPAKA RISES.` · then, large: `HE SPENDS HIS WISH ON FORGIVENESS.`

segments.voice: Many pujas end with a short prayer asking God to forgive whatever we got wrong. Ask that for yourself first. Then bring to mind someone who hurt you, not the worst hurt, something middle-sized, and if you can, wish them well in one plain sentence: may they be well. If you don't pray, just say the sentence, and notice what it costs and what it frees.
Pushpaka. Kubera's flying chariot, once taken by Ravana, now carries Rama home, after he spends his one wish on forgiveness for Kaikeyi and Bharata.
Your line: forgiveness is part of dharma. Rama spent his one wish on it. Tomorrow, the road home in reverse. Day six hundred sixty, done.
